evidence.claims: Checked: the 6-row Table A, B, C, D numbers in README match results.txt (pass); 'about 9,100' for 9,138 (pass); 'every parameter is assumed' disclosed (pass); Wright 1936 'cited from memory, not fetched' disclosed (pass). Fail: README:37 'the learning surcharge is under 8% after 200 coats' — 14.944/13.818 = 1.0815, an 8.15% surcharge, so the claim is false (it reads under 8% only from the rounded 14.9/13.8); the same sentence ships on the live page. Fail: README calls t(n)=t1*n^b a 'Wright learning curve' and attributes 'unit time falls by a fixed share with each doubling' to Wright (1936); Wright's model is the cumulative-average one, the unit-time form is Crawford's (1944). Under Wright's actual form the headline 20 coats (4x, 0.85) becomes 7, 96 becomes 33, 370 becomes 119 ({S}/indep2.py), so the misattribution changes the headline by about 3x and the README never says the model choice matters.
evidence.fitness: For a researcher: the result is a parameter sweep of a textbook learning curve where every input (first-coat multiple, rate, floor, materials) is assumed, and the README itself shows the answer spans three orders of magnitude on the two assumed numbers. Nearest prior work: Wright (1936), Crawford (1944, unit model), De Jong (1957, incompressible floor), Nembhard and Uzumeri (2000, measured learning and forgetting for sewing operators in a textile plant), Jaber and Bonney (1996, learn-forget curve). Only Wright is cited; nothing measured or sourced. Nothing here is new and there is no data to build on; it is a worked example, far from research/CLAUDE.md's PhD bar of multi-session programmes aimed at papers.
evidence.domain: Against standard learning-curve practice: the floor as max(floor, t1*n^b) is a crude version of De Jong's incompressibility model t1*(M+(1-M)n^b), which is the standard way to model a plateau and avoids the kink; the model form (unit vs cumulative-average) is not stated or tested though practitioners always name it; apparel learning rates exist in the IE literature and were not used; forgetting, which dominates for a hobbyist sewing intermittently, is excluded (disclosed). The arithmetic of the chosen model is right; the method choices a practitioner would question are unaddressed.

defects.what: The unit-time curve t(n)=t1*n^b is called a 'Wright learning curve' and attributed to Wright (1936); Wright's model is cumulative-average (the unit form is Crawford 1944). The choice is not stated as a choice, and under Wright's actual form the headline 20 coats becomes 7 (96 -> 33, 370 -> 119), so the headline depends on an unacknowledged model choice by ~3x.

Every parameter is assumed and no prior work on measured apparel/sewing learning rates, plateau (De Jong 1957) or forgetting (Jaber and Bonney 1996; Nembhard and Uzumeri 2000 studied sewing operators) is cited, so the result is a textbook sweep with nothing new for a researcher to build on.
'the learning surcharge is under 8% after 200 coats' is false: 14.944/13.818 = 8.15% (it looks under 8% only from rounded 14.9/13.8). Also served on the live page.
No test pins any results.txt number; 3 of 4 seeded mutants survive, including a wrong divisor in average_cost_over that drives all of Table D.
Table D is labelled 'sewing labour' but uses sewing + cutting minutes (76, not 51).

verdict: Does not meet the bar (claims 2, verification 2, median 2). The arithmetic is right: results.txt reproduces byte for byte and independent closed-form and hand recomputation matches every number in Tables A to D. But the README attributes a unit-time curve to Wright, whose model is cumulative-average, and under Wright's actual form the headline '20 coats' is 7; one prose claim ('under 8% after 200 coats') is false at 8.15%; three of four seeded bugs survive the tests; and as research it is a sweep of a 1930s-40s textbook model with every input assumed and the apparel learning-curve literature uncited, so there is nothing new or measured to build on.
